question: Keira assumes he's the new marketing hire. What's going on in that exchange?

options.text: She read him as non-technical before he'd said anything about his work
options.note: The assumption arrives first and the evidence never catches up. That's why it's tiring — the correction has to happen before the conversation can even start.

options.text: When he corrects her, she treats it as amusing rather than as information
options.note: "Oh, that's cute" keeps him in the role she assigned him. Being corrected didn't change her read of him. It just made the read more entertaining.

options.text: Getting someone's role wrong is an easy mistake and there's nothing more to it
options.note: It would be, once. What makes it a pattern is how she responds to being corrected — that part isn't a mix-up.

options.text: He should have led with his job title before she had a chance to assume
options.note: This puts the work on him to pre-empt everyone else's assumptions. Consider how much of his day that would take.

options.text: She said it in front of other people instead of quietly to him
options.note: An audience makes it sting more, but it would be the same assumption said alone in a lift.

options.text: She's senior to him, so she's entitled to size up a new hire
options.note: Seniority covers assessing his work. It doesn't cover deciding what kind of person he is on sight.

question: She comments on his shirt, then asks whether his girlfriend knows he dresses like that. What's the problem?

options.text: His body became the subject of a work conversation he didn't open
options.note: He came to talk about engineering. The topic got changed to how he looks, and he doesn't get a vote on that.

options.text: Competence got attached to appearance instead of to anything he's built
options.note: "Too tight for an engineer" makes the shirt the qualification. Nothing about his actual work ever comes up.

options.text: The girlfriend question assumes his private life, then asks him to account for it
options.note: Two things at once — it decides who he'd be with, and it makes his relationship something he now has to manage at work.

options.text: The shirt genuinely was too tight for a professional setting
options.note: Even if you'd have worn something else, that's a dress-code conversation with a manager. It isn't a remark about his body on the floor.

options.text: It would have been fine if she'd raised it with him privately
options.note: Somewhere quieter doesn't change what's being said. Private mostly means no witnesses.

options.text: He should have laughed it off to keep things comfortable
options.note: He can, and the story lets him. Notice that the cost of keeping things comfortable is only ever paid by him.

question: Chesca is standing right there and says nothing. What would bystander action have looked like?

options.text: Naming it in the moment, even lightly, so he isn't the only one who noticed
options.note: It doesn't take a confrontation. "He's an engineer, Keira" does most of the work, and it moves the cost off him.

options.text: Turning the conversation back to his actual role and what he's working on
options.note: Low risk and effective. It corrects the record without needing anyone to be the villain.

options.text: Checking in with him afterwards about what he'd like to happen next
options.note: Not a substitute for the moment, but it matters — and it leaves the decision with him.

options.text: Reporting it to HR straight away without saying anything to either of them
options.note: It skips past him entirely. A process starts, he hears about it later, and he had no say in any of it.

options.text: Waiting and raising it with Keira privately another day
options.note: Better than nothing, and it might even change Keira. It still leaves him standing alone in the room where it happened.

options.text: Staying out of it, since it wasn't said to her
options.note: Silence in the room reads as agreement to everyone in it — including him.

question: Someone wants to support him after this. What actually helps?

options.text: Listening, without arguing him out of how it landed
options.note: The fastest way to end the conversation is to explain to him why it wasn't that bad.

options.text: Letting him decide what happens next, including deciding nothing happens
options.note: Control is the thing that got taken. Handing it back is most of the job.

options.text: Telling him what support exists without requiring him to use it
options.note: Information rather than instruction. He can put it in his pocket and use it in six months.

options.text: Telling him not to take it personally
options.note: It was directed at him personally. This asks him to do the work of not minding.

options.text: Insisting he make a formal report right away
options.note: Well meant, and it takes the decision off him again — just in the other direction.

options.text: Promising to go and have it out with Keira on his behalf
options.note: Feels like solidarity. It's still someone else deciding what happens to him, and he's the one who wears the fallout.
